vignette:
# Robert's Morning Routine

Robert has been a cashier at the corner grocery for nineteen years. He arrives at 6:30 each morning, before the store opens, and performs the same ritual: he counts the register drawer three times, checks the back door lock twice, and positions himself behind the counter where he can see both the front entrance and the stockroom. His manager stopped commenting on this routine years ago.

This morning, like most mornings, Robert's hands shake slightly as he sorts the bills. He's seventy-six now, and his coworkers assume the tremor is simply age. He doesn't correct them. The truth is that his hands have shaken since 1992, when he was a journalist covering the siege in Sarajevo.

Robert remembers the assignment with crystalline clarity—the way the morning light looked through the damaged windows of the Holiday Inn, the smell of diesel fuel and something else he's never quite named. He was there to document the humanitarian crisis, to bear witness. On his eighth day, a mortar round struck the building's west wing. He was in the east wing, interviewing a woman about her missing son. The concussion threw him against the wall. He remembers the woman's face—her expression didn't change, as though explosions were simply part of the conversation now.

He made it out three days later. He filed his stories. He won an award. He told himself he was fine.

But he wasn't fine. The nightmares came first, then the hypervigilance. Loud noises sent his nervous system into overdrive. He couldn't sit with his back to a door. His first wife, Margaret, tried to understand, but after five years of his night terrors and his inability to be touched without flinching, she suggested he see someone. He refused. Men from his generation didn't talk about such things. He pushed through, as he'd been taught to do.

He eventually returned to journalism, but the work felt hollow. Every assignment felt like an accusation—that he should still be doing more, seeing more, witnessing more. The hypervigilance that had kept him alive in Sarajevo now made him unable to concentrate on writing. He left journalism at forty-two and became a cashier. It was supposed to be temporary.

Margaret died twelve years ago. Cancer. Robert was present for her death in a way he'd never quite managed while she was alive, and he's never forgiven himself for that.

Now, at the register, Robert watches customers approach. He notices their hands first—whether they're empty, whether they're trembling. He tracks the exits. When someone raises their voice in frustration about a price or a returned item, something in his chest tightens. Just last week, a teenager knocked over a display of cans near the front, and Robert found himself on the floor before he'd consciously decided to move. His coworker had to help him up.

He sleeps poorly most nights. The dreams are less vivid now than they were, but they're relentless—variations on the same theme of being trapped, of needing to protect someone he cannot reach. He wakes at 3 or 4 a.m. most mornings and reads in his apartment until it's time to come to work.

His daughter calls occasionally and asks if he's considered retirement. He tells her he's fine. The routine keeps him steady. The register, the counting, the vigilance—these are the things that make sense to him now. He's learned to live in the space between then and now, never quite settling into either.
